headings.title: Introduction to Body Support and Posture in Nursing
headings.content: Body support and posture form the physical foundation of safe nursing practice and patient care. Posture refers to the alignment of the body's parts—head, trunk, arms, and legs—while holding a position such as standing, sitting, or lying down. Proper posture maintains the body's center of gravity over its base of support, reducing physical strain on bones, joints, ligaments, and muscles. In clinical settings, nurses manage body support for two distinct groups: themselves during physically demanding tasks, and vulnerable patients who cannot maintain alignment independently due to weakness, paralysis, or altered consciousness.

headings.title: Anatomical Principles of Alignment and Balance
headings.content:
Body alignment, or posture, brings body parts into geometric harmony, minimizing stress on the musculoskeletal system. Balance is achieved when the center of gravity is close to the base of support, and the line of gravity passes vertically through the base of support. A wide base of support and a lower center of gravity increase stability and prevent falls or tipping.

- **Center of Gravity**: The point around which mass is evenly distributed, located centrally in the pelvis in anatomical position.
- **Base of Support**: The area beneath an object or person, bounded by the points of contact with the floor or surface.
- **Line of Gravity**: An imaginary vertical line passing through the center of gravity to the ground.

headings.title: Physiological Benefits of Proper Posture
headings.content: Maintaining optimal body alignment does more than prevent aches; it directly supports vital organ function. Proper spinal alignment expands the thoracic cavity, allowing full lung expansion and efficient gas exchange. Conversely, slumped postures compress the abdominal and thoracic organs, restricting diaphragmatic movement and reducing vital capacity. Good posture also prevents uneven pressure on articular cartilage, promotes efficient venous return from the lower extremities, and reduces excessive energy expenditure during movement.

headings.title: Factors Affecting Posture and Mobility
headings.content: Numerous variables influence a person's ability to maintain normal posture and move freely. Growth and development stages alter spinal curves from infancy to adulthood. Nutritional status, particularly calcium and vitamin D intake, determines bone density and structural integrity. Health status, pain, fatigue, and central nervous system integrity also play massive roles. Mental health conditions such as severe depression can manifest physically as a stooped, guarded posture.

headings.title: Common Postural Deformities and Musculoskeletal Complications
headings.content:
Prolonged poor posture, congenital conditions, or neuromuscular diseases can lead to permanent structural deformities. Nurses must recognize these conditions during physical assessments to plan effective interventions and prevent further deterioration.

- **Lordosis**: An exaggerated inward curvature of the lumbar spine, often called swayback.
- **Kyphosis**: An exaggerated outward curvature of the thoracic spine, commonly known as hunchback.
- **Scoliosis**: A lateral or sideways curvature of the spine that can be 'C' or 'S' shaped.
- **Foot Drop**: Plantar flexion contracture where the patient cannot dorsiflex the foot.

headings.title: Assessment of Patient Posture and Body Mechanics
headings.content: Evaluating a patient's posture requires a systematic physical assessment from multiple angles in standing, sitting, and lying positions. The nurse observes spinal curves, symmetry of shoulders and hips, alignment of extremities, and gait stability. Assessment also involves checking muscle strength, joint range of motion, and the presence of pain during movement. Findings help determine the patient's risk for falls and identify specific nursing diagnoses such as Impaired Physical Mobility or Risk for Injury.

headings.title: Principles of Safe Patient Handling and Body Mechanics for Nurses
headings.content: Using proper body mechanics protects nurses from debilitating back injuries. Key principles include maintaining a wide base of support, keeping loads close to the body's center of gravity, bending at the knees instead of the waist, and avoiding twisting of the spine during lifting. Whenever possible, nurses should push or slide objects rather than lift them, and utilize team lifting or mechanical lifts for heavy or dependent patients.

headings.title: Therapeutic Positioning Devices and Assistive Equipment
headings.content: Bedridden patients require specialized devices to maintain alignment, prevent pressure injuries, and avoid contractures. Pillows, trochanter rolls, footboards, and hand rolls are standard positioning aids. Mechanical lifts, transfer boards, and gait belts assist nurses in moving patients safely without risking injury to either party. Using these tools distributes body weight evenly and keeps joints in functional alignment during prolonged immobility.
